blocks.quote: From Mythos to Logos: The Mental Landscape That Made Computation Thinkable
blocks.section: From Mythos to Logos: The Mental Landscape That Made Computation Thinkable

blocks.quote: The physical prerequisites are the silicon, the cables, the cooling. Beneath them lies a *mental* layer: the habits of thought that made a reasoning machine conceivable. They were not invented for computation. They were invented to explain the sky, to justify the rule of kings, to calculate the tides, and to win at dice. The same logic that classified Greek gods now classifies the layers of a neural network; the same probability that priced a 17th-century gamble now trains a language model.
blocks.section: From Mythos to Logos: The Mental Landscape That Made Computation Thinkable

blocks.quote: The Mythos: How Story Shaped the Mind
blocks.section: The Mythos: How Story Shaped the Mind

blocks.quote: Before science, there was story. Every pre-scientific civilisation explained the natural world through **mythos**: narratives in which gods, spirits, and cosmic beings directly caused natural phenomena. The sun was a chariot driven across the sky; the seasons were the result of a god's moods; earthquakes were the anger of a deity beneath the earth. This was not "wrong" in the modern sense; it was a *different kind of model*, one in which agency was located in personal beings rather than in impersonal laws.
blocks.section: The Mythos: How Story Shaped the Mind

blocks.quote: Yet mythos was not merely an obstacle to science. It created specific mental prerequisites without which the scientific revolution would have been unthinkable:
blocks.section: The Mythos: How Story Shaped the Mind

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_great_chain_of_being_1579} (Public Domain): the hierarchy of creation as \citeauthor{img_great_chain_of_being_1579} drew it in Rhetorica Christiana — from inert matter at the base, through plants, animals, and humans, up through the angels to God at the apex. The fixed, ranked ladder that dominated Western thought for a millennium, the last great echo of which is Linnaeus's Systema Naturae . Source: \citeauthor{img_great_chain_of_being_1579}, \citeyear{img_great_chain_of_being_1579}, \citealternativetitle{img_great_chain_of_being_1579}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: The Mythos: How Story Shaped the Mind

blocks.quote: The Birth of Natural Philosophy: From Thales to Archimedes
blocks.section: The Birth of Natural Philosophy: From Thales to Archimedes

blocks.quote: The transition from mythos to **logos** (λόγος), from story to reasoned argument, began in the Greek city-states of Ionia in the 6th century BCE. The Milesian natural philosophers, **Thales of Miletus** (c. 624–546 BCE), **Anaximander** (c. 610–546 BCE), and **Anaximenes** (c. 586–526 BCE), made a move that had no precedent in any prior tradition: they proposed that natural phenomena could be explained without reference to the will of gods. Thales argued that water was the fundamental substance (*arche*) of all things; Anaximander proposed the boundless (*apeiron*); Anaximenes proposed air. These explanations were, by modern standards, wrong. But the *form* of the explanation, a natural cause operating according to a natural principle, was a revolution.
blocks.section: The Birth of Natural Philosophy: From Thales to Archimedes

blocks.quote: The Islamic Golden Age: The Bridge
blocks.section: The Islamic Golden Age: The Bridge

blocks.quote: Between the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the European Renaissance, the centre of gravity of scientific thought shifted to the Islamic world. The scholars of the **Abbasid Caliphate** (750–1258 CE) did not merely preserve Greek texts; they extended them, corrected them, and applied them in ways the Greeks had not imagined.
blocks.section: The Islamic Golden Age: The Bridge

blocks.quote: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687
blocks.section: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687

blocks.quote: The Scientific Revolution was not a single event but a cascade of mutually reinforcing breakthroughs, each one displacing the last:
blocks.section: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687

blocks.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_copernicus_portrait} (CC BY 4.0): Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), whose De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (\citeyear{copernicus1543revolutionibus}) displaced the Earth from the centre of the cosmos — the first and most consequential displacement in the Scientific Revolution. Source: \citeauthor{img_copernicus_portrait}, \citeyear{img_copernicus_portrait}, \citealternativetitle{img_copernicus_portrait}, Wikimedia Commons.
blocks.section: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687

blocks.quote: But it was the suppressed \citetitle{descartes1664lemonde} (\citeyear{descartes1664lemonde}), published posthumously, that contained the deeper displacement. Descartes proposed that the physical world, including the human body, is a **machine** (*horologium*): a self-operating mechanism governed by the same mechanical laws as a clock. Animals are automata; the body, after death, is a machine that has stopped. The *soul* (or mind, *res cogitans*) is non-physical and cannot be a machine. But the *body* is. This is the seed of the "brain as computer" idea: if the body is clockwork, then the question "can the thinking part also be a mechanism?" becomes coherent. Descartes kept the soul off the machine, but he put the organism on it. The step from "the body is a machine" to "the brain is a computer" was taken, in mathematics, by \citeauthorlastnameand{mccullochpitts1943} in \citeyear{mccullochpitts1943}; in engineering, by the designers of the first neural networks.
blocks.section: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687

blocks.quote: The *Principia* also contained the first rigorous formulation of **calculus** (independent of Leibniz's), the mathematical machinery for describing change. Without calculus, there is no differential equation; without differential equations, there is no differential geometry, no action principle, no variational method, and no of the optimization algorithms that train a neural network.
blocks.section: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687

blocks.quote: Leibniz also independently invented the **calculus** (derivatives and integrals) in the 1670s, publishing his notation ($\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\int$) in 1684, three years before Newton's *Principia*. The priority dispute that followed was bitter and prolonged, but the substance of the contribution is clear: Leibniz's notation, still in use today, was the one that proved more general and more suitable for computation.
blocks.section: The Scientific Revolution: 1543–1687

blocks.quote: The Mathematical Infrastructure of Computation
blocks.section: The Mathematical Infrastructure of Computation

blocks.quote: The Scientific Revolution provided the *physical* model of the world. The *mathematical* infrastructure for modern computation was built in parallel, by people working on problems that had nothing to do with machines:
blocks.section: The Mathematical Infrastructure of Computation

blocks.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{bayes1763essay} died in 1761, leaving behind a manuscript, "An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances," which his friend Richard Price discovered and published in the *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society* in \citeyear{bayes1763essay}. The essay solves a problem of **inverse probability**: given the data, what is the probability of the hypothesis that generated it? This is **Bayesian inference**, and it is the mathematical engine of every probabilistic machine learning model, from the Perceptron's update rule to the variational autoencoder.
blocks.section: The Mathematical Infrastructure of Computation

blocks.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{laplace1812analytic}'s \citetitle{laplace1812analytic} (\citeyear{laplace1812analytic}) independently derived and generalized Bayes's result, unified probability with the theory of errors, and applied it to astronomical prediction. His \citetitle{laplace1814essai} (\citeyear{laplace1814essai}) added the **Laplace demon** and the **central limit theorem**, the result that the sum of a large number of independent random variables tends toward a Gaussian distribution. The central limit theorem is the reason that **backpropagation** works: the gradient of a loss function over millions of parameters is a sum of many small, roughly independent contributions, and its distribution is approximately Gaussian, which is why the stochastic gradient estimator is so effective.
blocks.section: The Mathematical Infrastructure of Computation

blocks.quote: The bridge from Boolean algebra to physical circuits was built by \citeauthorlastnameand{shannon1938relay} in his MIT master's thesis, "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits," published in the *Transactions of the AIEE* in \citeyear{shannon1938relay}. Shannon showed that Boole's algebra is **isomorphic** to the algebra of two-state electrical circuits: AND is switches in series; OR is switches in parallel; NOT is an inverter. A logical formula can be *wired into a physical circuit*, and the circuit can *compute* the truth value of the formula. This is the moment at which logic became hardware. Without Shannon's 1938 thesis, the digital computer is a philosophical curiosity; with it, it is an engineering discipline.
blocks.section: The Mathematical Infrastructure of Computation

blocks.quote: The Convergence
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: The transition from mythos to computation is not one invention but the **convergence of five independent intellectual revolutions**:
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: | Revolution | Key Figures | Concept Contributed | Where It Lives in an LLM |
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: | **Classification** (Aristotle → Linnaeus → Darwin) | Aristotle, Linnaeus, Darwin | Discrete, nested, ranked categories; then the **tree** | Type systems; hierarchical organization of information |
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: | **Mechanism** (Descartes → Newton → Laplace) | Descartes, Newton, Laplace | The world (incl. the brain) as a **deterministic, rule-governed mechanism** | The computer as a mechanism; the "brain as computer" idea |
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: | **Probability** (Pascal/Fermat → Bayes → Laplace) | Pascal, Fermat, Bayes, Laplace | A calculus of **uncertainty** | Statistical learning; inference under noise; all of probabilistic ML |
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: | **Logic as Algebra** (Boole → Shannon) | Boole, De Morgan, Peirce, Shannon | Logic as **symbolic algebra** → realizable in **switches** | The logic gate; the digital circuit; computation as wired logic |
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: | **Information** (Telegraph → Shannon 1948) | Morse, Shannon | **Information** as a quantifiable, transmissible quantity | The bit; coding; error correction; the "content" of data |
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: Each of these revolutions was driven by problems that had nothing to do with computation: how to classify the animals of the known world, how to justify the divine order, how to divide the stakes in an interrupted game, how to wire a telegraph switch, how to measure the capacity of a communication channel. Yet together, they produced the *mental landscape* in which the idea of a machine that reasons became not only possible but inevitable. The LLM is the endpoint of a convergence that began when a Greek philosopher in Miletus looked at the sea and decided that it did not need a god to explain it.
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: Ideas alone do not compute. Every inference rests on a scaffold of discoveries made by people who never imagined a machine writing poetry — the displaced prerequisites that fill the rest of this history.
blocks.section: The Convergence

blocks.quote: From Foragers to Civilisations: The Sedentarisation That Made Computation Thinkable
blocks.section: From Foragers to Civilisations: The Sedentarisation That Made Computation Thinkable

blocks.quote: The **Neolithic Revolution**, the wide-scale shift from nomadic foraging to settled agriculture beginning around 11,700 years ago, is the largest single change in the human niche since the spread of *Homo erectus*. The very idea that such a prehistoric shift could be called a *revolution* comes from **V. Gordon Childe** (\citeauthor{childe1936man}), who argued in his 1936 *Man Makes Himself* that the British population curve between 1750 and 1800 turns "through an angle of about 30°," and that comparable kinks far enough back in prehistory deserve the same name (\cite[Childe 1936, ch. 1]{childe1936man_txt}). He later labelled two of those kinks the **Neolithic Revolution** and the **Urban Revolution** (\cite[Childe 1950]{childe1950urban}). Without **sedentarisation** (*Sesshaftwerdung*), none of the intellectual and material prerequisites of modern computation could have emerged.
blocks.section: From Foragers to Civilisations: The Sedentarisation That Made Computation Thinkable

blocks.quote: From foraging to farming
blocks.section: From foraging to farming

blocks.quote: For the vast majority of their existence, humans were foragers: small, mobile bands that owned few possessions and consumed food within days of gathering it. Australian Aboriginal foragers of the Western Desert, ethnographically studied in the twentieth century, sustained extraordinarily detailed oral traditions for at least 65,000 years — but the lifestyle imposed a hard ceiling on every other dimension of accumulation.
blocks.section: From foraging to farming

blocks.quote: Without stored food, there could be no fixed residence, no pottery, no granaries, no dense craft specialisation, no civic buildings, no writing, no standing armies, no taxation — and no libraries, no schools, and no project that outlasted the working life of a single forager.
blocks.section: From foraging to farming

blocks.quote: The change began with the climate. As the Pleistocene ice sheets melted, the climate wobbled through a final cold snap (the **Younger Dryas**, ~10,900–9,700 BCE) and then settled into the long, warm, stable interval we still inhabit, the **Holocene**. What made the **Fertile Crescent** special was not a single miracle crop but a *package* of eight wild species — the **Neolithic founder crops** identified by **Daniel Zohary** with Maria Hopf and later Ehud Weiss (\cite[Zohary, Hopf & Weiss 2012]{zoharyhopf2000domestication}): the cereals emmer, einkorn, and barley; the pulses lentil, pea, chickpea, and bitter vetch; and the fibre plant flax.
blocks.section: From foraging to farming

blocks.quote: The earliest secure evidence for cultivated, morphologically domesticated emmer and einkorn comes from sites in the Fertile Crescent at roughly 9500 BCE, before pottery, before towns, and before writing. Sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs followed; stored grain and managed herds made a year-round sedentary diet possible for the first time.
blocks.section: From foraging to farming

blocks.quote: The first towns
blocks.section: The first towns

blocks.quote: Sedentarisation preceded agriculture, not the other way around. The site of **Jericho** (\cite[Kenyon 1957]{kenyon1957digging}), in the West Bank near a perennial spring, has stone-walled occupation layers beginning in the **Pre-Pottery Neolithic A** around 9500 BCE — earlier than full cereal domestication. Its Neolithic tower (c. 8000 BCE, ~8.5 m tall) is one of the oldest stone monuments on Earth, and its surrounding wall and ditch are the earliest known example of **fortification**, a built structure whose purpose is to defend a *fixed place*.
blocks.section: The first towns

blocks.quote: A few hundred kilometres north, in the Konya plain, **Çatalhöyük** (\cite[Mellaart 1967]{mellaart1967catal}) was occupied from roughly 7500 to 5600 BCE and at its peak housed somewhere between 600 and 8,000 people, the largest known Neolithic proto-city. The second, much longer campaign under **Ian Hodder** (1993–2018) overturned Mellaart's "Mother Goddess" reading: only one of ~2,000 figurines matched the Mother Goddess style, fewer than five percent depicted women, and the houses were remarkably uniform in size with no clear hierarchical elite (\cite[Hodder 2006]{hodder2006leopard}).
blocks.section: The first towns

blocks.quote: The Urban Revolution and the metals
blocks.section: The Urban Revolution and the metals

blocks.quote: Childe's second coinage, the **Urban Revolution** (\cite[Childe 1950]{childe1950urban}), names what happened around 4000 BCE in southern Mesopotamia: the small farming villages of the Uruk period coalesced into cities. **Uruk** itself grew to perhaps 50,000 inhabitants by 3100 BCE; comparable trajectories played out in Egypt, the Indus valley, the Yellow River basin, and later Mesoamerica.
blocks.section: The Urban Revolution and the metals

blocks.quote: In a 1950 *Town Planning Review* paper, Childe listed ten diagnostic features of the first cities — large population, full-time specialists, concentration of surplus, monumental architecture, a ruling class freed from manual labour, systems of recording and writing, exact and predictive sciences, representational art, long-distance trade, and a state organisation based on residence rather than kinship (\cite[Childe 1950]{childe1950urban}) — almost every one of which is a step in the chain that ends at a printed circuit.
blocks.section: The Urban Revolution and the metals

blocks.quote: Cities needed metal. The **Bronze Age** — Near East c. 3300–1200 BCE — ran on long-distance trade in tin and copper; Childe, in *Man Makes Himself*, makes the deeper argument about why: "The bronze axe which replaces it is not only a superior implement, it also presupposes a more complex economic and social structure. The casting of bronze is too difficult a process to be carried out by anyone in the intervals of growing or catching his food or minding her babies. It is a specialist's job, and these specialists must rely for such primary necessities as food upon a surplus produced by other specialists. Again, the copper and tin of which the bronze axe is composed are comparatively rare, and very seldom occur together. One or both of the constituents will almost certainly have to be imported. Such importation is possible only if some sort of communications and trade have been established and if there is a surplus of some local product to barter for the metals" (\cite[Childe 1936, ch. 1]{childe1936man_txt}).
blocks.section: The Urban Revolution and the metals

blocks.quote: Writing, law, libraries
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: The single most consequential innovation of the Urban Revolution for this lesson is **writing**. It emerged not from literary ambition but from bookkeeping.
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: In **Denise Schmandt-Besserat**'s reconstruction, the first system was a set of small shaped clay **tokens** — cones, spheres, disks, cylinders — in use across the Near East from the eighth millennium BCE. Her original 1978 paper in *Scientific American* put the thesis crisply: "Long before the Sumerians invented writing, accounts in western Asia were kept with clay tokens of various distinctive shapes. It appears that the tokens gave rise to the Sumerian ideographs" (\cite[Schmandt-Besserat 1978]{schmandtbesserat1978}; \cite[Schmandt-Besserat 1992]{schmandtbesserat1992}; \cite[Schmandt-Besserat 1996]{schmandtbesserat1996}).
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: Tokens sealed inside clay *bullae* were marked on the outside with their own shapes — the first case of a physical record carrying its own verification. Around 3300 BCE, in Uruk IV, the envelope was dropped for a flat tablet on which the token shapes were impressed directly; by 2600 BCE the picture-shapes had been replaced by the wedge-shaped marks we call **cuneiform**, from the Latin *cuneus*.
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: Cuneiform was the first of five independent inventions of writing: Egyptian **hieroglyphs** (c. 3200 BCE), undeciphered Indus script (c. 2600 BCE), Shang Chinese oracle-bone characters (c. 1250 BCE), and Mesoamerican **Maya** (c. 300 BCE).
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: The next question after cities was how to make a king's word outlast the king. The **Code of Hammurabi** (\cite[Roth 1997]{roth1997lawcollections}; \cite[Scheil 1902]{scheil1902code}) is the earliest preserved answer: a basalt stele ~2.25 m tall, inscribed in Old Babylonian Akkadian around 1753 BCE, rediscovered at Susa in 1901, edited by the Dominican priest **Jean-Vincent Scheil** in 1902, and now in the Louvre.
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: Its 282 case-form laws cover everything from a surgeon's fee to *lex talionis* — "an eye for an eye." The principle most modern readers remember is the second; the more durable contribution is structural: a body of law, made public on a monument in every major city of the empire, that could be cited after the king's death.
blocks.section: Writing, law, libraries

blocks.quote: Why sedentarisation is a prerequisite of AI
blocks.section: Why sedentarisation is a prerequisite of AI

blocks.quote: Strip any one element out of this chain and the rest cannot stand. No agriculture, no fixed residence; no fixed residence, no pottery, no granary, no city; no city, no specialised scribal class; no scribal class, no writing; no writing, no codified law, no coinage, no algebra, no astronomy accurate enough to predict eclipses, no geometry accurate enough to survey after a Nile flood, no library, no encyclopedia, no standard mathematical notation, no "algorithm" in the modern sense.
blocks.section: Why sedentarisation is a prerequisite of AI

blocks.quote: Each step was made for reasons that had nothing to do with computation. Yet the chain they collectively built is the chain on which every calculator, database, operating system, and large language model rests. A language model is a model of human *language*, and human language was *first made durable* by the scribes of Sumer.
blocks.section: Why sedentarisation is a prerequisite of AI

blocks.quote: The grammatical categories of Akkadian and Sumerian, the case system of Latin, the inflectional morphology of ancient Greek, the tonal layers of Middle Chinese, the analytic structure of Old English — all of these are inside the corpus on which an LLM is trained, because they were inside the libraries that writing built, that agriculture made possible, that the cities of the first urban revolution sustained. Take the chain away and the corpus thins to oral memory; take the oral memory away and the model has nothing to model.
blocks.section: Why sedentarisation is a prerequisite of AI
